issues.legal_issue: A landowner cannot recover land declared surplus merely because the government has not yet used it to resettle tenants.
material_facts: A competent authority declared part of the landowner’s holding surplus, and the declaration became final after appeal and revision proceedings.
The surplus land had not been used by the government to resettle tenants when the landowner sought to prevent its use.
issues.conclusion: The landowner could not reclaim the surplus land on the ground that it had not been utilised; the government retained the right to use it for tenant resettlement without a time limit.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 9(1)(i) and 10A(a) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, the government may use surplus land to resettle tenants ejected or liable to be ejected, and a final surplus declaration gives the government an indefeasible right to do so. The Act sets no time limit for that use and gives the owner no right to restoration merely because use has been delayed. Sections 10A(b) and 10B provide limited exceptions concerning acquisition and inheritance; those exceptions do not create a general right to recover land because of non-use.

predicates.surplus_area_proceeding: The proceeding determines land surplus to a landowner’s permissible area for potential use in resettling tenants.
predicates.final_surplus_order: The competent authority made a surplus-land declaration that became final.
predicates.surplus_land_not_yet_utilized: The government had not yet used the declared surplus land to resettle tenants.

issues.definition: When a final surplus-land declaration has not yet been implemented in a surplus-area proceeding, the delay alone does not restore the land to its owner.

issues.legal_issue: Reorganisation of a state does not extinguish a final surplus-land order made before reorganisation or entitle a landowner to a separate permissible area in each successor state.
material_facts: Before reorganisation, a final order declared part of the landowner’s holding surplus under the applicable land-tenure law.
The landowner’s properties fell within two successor states after reorganisation, and the declared surplus land had not yet been used.
The landowner claimed a separate permissible area in each successor state and argued that the unimplemented order should no longer have effect.
issues.conclusion: The pre-reorganisation surplus-land order remained effective and could be implemented after reorganisation; the landowner was not entitled to separate permissible areas in the successor states.
issues.legal_principle: Section 88 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 continued the prior law in the territories to which it had applied before reorganisation, while section 89 authorised adaptation of laws. Clauses 10 and 11 of the Haryana Adaptation of Laws (States and Concurrent Subjects) Order, 1968 preserved prior orders, acts, rights, and liabilities. Read together, these provisions allowed both successor states to give effect to a final pre-reorganisation surplus order despite the division of the land. The court also rejected a separate-ceiling claim as inconsistent with the statutory scheme and detrimental to tenants needing resettlement.

predicates.interstate_reorganisation_surplus_area_c: The case concerns the effect of state reorganisation on a surplus-area proceeding.
predicates.pre_reorganisation_surplus_order_final: A surplus-land order became final before the state reorganisation.
predicates.landholding_divided_between_successor_st: The landowner’s holding fell within more than one successor state after reorganisation.

issues.definition: When a final surplus-land order predates reorganisation and the holding is divided between successor states, the order remains effective and does not give the owner separate permissible areas in those states.
